Smoothing scales and prescribed normal jets

Written by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), October 2026. Public domain (CC0).

Smoothing at a scale proportional to the distance from a plane can supply derivatives that the boundary data do not have. Multiplication by a suitable normal monomial compensates for the derivatives of that changing scale. This gives extensions of finite jets with exactly the necessary tangential regularity. For an infinite smooth jet, a different construction uses successively thinner cutoff layers; no convergence of the formal Taylor series is required.

The normal-jet extension, Lemma 2.1 and formulas (2.3)–(2.8), proves the compact-data extension, including the moment-cancelling kernel and every mixed derivative estimate. We use that construction to obtain an extension for arbitrary data with local seminorm bounds. The scalar foundation, Sections 13.3–13.5, 13.7 and 13.10, supplies the fundamental theorem, finite-coordinate differentiation, uniform convergence of differentiated series and smooth cutoffs. The integration foundation, Sections 15.1 and 16, supplies substitution, product integration and dominated convergence. The integral Taylor formula supplies the finite Taylor expansions used below.

We use ordinary derivatives. Tangential variables are ; a scalar normal variable is , and a normal vector is . Multi-indices have nonnegative integer entries, , and . The support of a function on an open set is the relative closure of its nonzero set.

The scales in this proof depend on the data. Linearity of the finite extension (J13) does not establish linearity or continuity of this infinite-jet construction. Only existence and the stated support and trace properties have been asserted.

Smooth data on an arbitrary open base

Corollary 4 (local bounds suffice for an infinite jet). If is open and are arbitrary, there is with every trace . Its normal support can be confined to a fixed compact neighborhood of zero. Tangential compact support is not asserted.

Proof. The empty open set is immediate. Choose increasing compact sets which contain every compact subset of for all sufficiently large . When , use the closed balls of integer radius. Otherwise use The distance function is continuous and 1-Lipschitz, by the triangle inequality. These sets are closed and bounded, hence compact, and are contained in . A compact subset of has positive distance from its closed complement: choose a ball in around each point, use finitely many half-radius balls to cover the compact set, and take the minimum of their positive half radii. It is also bounded. These two facts prove the required exhaustion property.

Use (J17) with on . For , impose (J19) only on , using all derivatives through order . Those finitely many seminorms are finite; the same positive powers of permit the choice. On any fixed compact base set and at any fixed derivative order , all sufficiently large degrees satisfy both and . Thus the derivative series converge uniformly on that compact set, with the summable bound . There are only finitely many terms of the excluded degrees. The local uniform derivative-series theorem gives smoothness on , and (J21) proves every trace. The same fixed cutoff confines the normal support.

Exercises with complete solutions

Exercise 1 (introductory: the second trace). In dimension one let , , and . Compute and the first four normal traces of , of orders zero through three.

Solution. Expanding the polynomial gives The traces are respectively . They verify (J3), including the signs and factorials. In particular, an arbitrary mollifier creates higher normal traces; the recursion (J14) accounts for them.

Exercise 2 (intermediate: rough highest data). Prescribe , , on . Construct a extension using Lemma 1. Explain why is not such an extension on the whole plane and why no extension with these traces can be .

Solution. Take any compact smooth integral-one kernel and set . Lemma 1 with gives , , and . For any fixed , the function has different left and right derivatives at , so it is not there. If an extension were , its first normal derivative restricted to the plane would be in , contradicting the nondifferentiability of at zero. Thus the required regularity of the highest trace is exact.

Exercise 3 (intermediate: positive kernels and moments). Show that a nonnegative smooth integral-one kernel on cannot have zero second moment. Starting with an even such kernel , construct a signed kernel with integral one and both first and second moments zero.

Solution. A nonnegative continuous kernel with integral one is positive on some open interval containing a nonzero point. The integral of over a smaller such interval is positive. Thus its second moment cannot be zero. Let . Both integrals equal one, both first moments vanish by evenness, and the second moment of is four times that of . Consequently has all the requested moments. This explains the allowance of signed kernels in (J13).

Exercise 5 (advanced: divergent Taylor data). Let with , and prescribe for one normal variable. Show that Theorem 3 realizes these data, although the formal Taylor series at converges at no nonzero normal argument.

Solution. All data have support in the fixed compact , so Theorem 3 applies for any compact normal neighborhood. At , the formal series has terms . For fixed , the ratio of successive absolute values is , eventually greater than two. In particular its terms do not tend to zero, which is necessary for convergence since each term is the difference of consecutive partial sums. The constructed function is smooth but cannot be analytic in the normal variable at this point.

Exercise 6 (advanced: widths chosen without the data). Fix any positive sequence and a compact smooth cutoff equal to one near zero. Show that using these widths in cannot realize every scalar jet by a uniformly convergent series.

Solution. Choose so small that , and put . At , the -th summand equals . These points eventually lie in any fixed compact neighborhood of zero, so the suprema of the individual terms there do not tend to zero. Uniform convergence of a series would force its terms to converge uniformly to zero, by subtracting consecutive partial sums. Hence this choice fails. It does not contradict Theorem 3: its widths are selected after the data are known.

Exercise 7 (intermediate: two normal coordinates). Let , , and suppose the only nonzero datum is . Write (J13) and all its normal traces through order two. Give the tangential support bound when .

Solution. With the moment kernel through degree two, Theorem 2 gives . Its value, two first derivatives and two pure second normal derivatives are zero on the plane. Its mixed derivative is ; the reversed derivative is the same by regularity. If the kernel and normal cutoff have radii , its support has tangential projection in . No derivatives of are required.

Exercise 8 (advanced: necessity and nonuniqueness). Prove that the regularities in (J10) are necessary for the traces of any function. Show also that an infinite smooth jet does not determine a unique smooth extension, even with a prescribed compact support neighborhood.

Solution. If , then is ; restricting to and taking its tangential derivatives gives exactly that regularity for the trace. For nonuniqueness choose nonzero compact smooth functions and , with supported inside the requested normal neighborhood and equal to one near zero. The scalar foundation's flat function is for , and zero for ; all its derivatives at zero are zero. The function is smooth by composition and the product rule. Every normal derivative at vanishes, while is not identically zero. Adding preserves every prescribed trace. When a fixed tangential compact is required, this example applies whenever contains the support of a nonzero smooth , for example when has nonempty interior. No nonzero such example is asserted for a compact set with empty interior.
